A second, independent tower: integer and fractions

This tower shows fraction multiplication and a failed construction. A fraction with a zero denominator fails as invalid. Natural numbers feed repeat, then multiplication and fraction multiplication. Fractions also feed fraction multiplication. The seen-value observation reads the result through the granted value probe. It does not call fraction multiplication. Outcomes come from core runs at build time. Explore the integer world.

  1. L1 Core summary: Natural numbers keep nonnegative integers. Bounded (61 cases)
  2. L2 Core summary: Repeat applies a supplied operation to a seed the requested number of times. Uses Nat. Bounded (50 cases)
  3. L3 Core summary: Multiplication counts ticks, adds the left magnitude once per tick, and negates the result when input signs differ. Uses Nat, @repeat. Bounded (169 cases)
  4. L1 Core summary: Fractions reject a zero denominator and reduce numerator and denominator with a consistent sign. Bounded (169 cases)
  5. L4 Core summary: Fraction multiplication multiplies the numerators and denominators, then constructs a reduced fraction. Uses Frac, mul. Bounded (100 cases)
  6. L1 Printed from the core definition (re-parses: yes): obs ?seen_value{value} = ?value{value} L1. Bounded (21 cases)
  7. Frac<1, 0> Executable (core run artifact) returns Bottom(invalid) through the core.

Each row has bounded evidence from the versioned run artifact. The prose summaries describe these core definitions, not the longer twelve-card story design text. Only the printed row is pasteable source.

docs.title: Challenge v2 catalogue
docs.text: v2.json uses schema opulse.challenge_v2/3. Regenerate with PYTHONPATH=src python tools/tasks_v2_challenge.py. This is a standalone catalogue, not a replacement for the currently loaded challenge JSON. The existing challenge.js does not load this file, and challenge-check.js only offers interpreter calls (evaluate, steps, equivalent, size), not a task-v2 grader. The browser cannot grade these tasks without a service.

docs.title: Top-level fields
docs.text:
• schema: constant opulse.challenge_v2/3; previous versions exposed references or answer checks and must not be served.
  • challenges: empty array for the legacy audit that scans this directory.
  • grading_sha256: SHA-256 of the exact bytes of the locally rebuilt, untracked grading JSON. It is a content check, not an answer or answer hash.
  • distribution: counts at levels 1 through 5 for all generated candidates, before quality and uniqueness filtering. Seed 104729 keeps the challenge candidates disjoint from committed samples. The operation pool uses indices 0..23 per world/angle; other kinds use 16 indices per angle. Templates also include their 15 concrete cases in every angle; the generic computer source contributes three per angle where valid. Frozen sample questions are excluded from selection. Candidates whose canonical world/angle/kind/question hash or UTF-8 prompt hash appears in tools/challenge_v2_retired.json are also excluded: earlier repository history exposed their answer checks. The authored path uses fresh inputs and prompts for the same reason. The retired manifest contains hashes only.
  • ladders: keys compute, invert, decide, describe, induce, create. Each starts at level 3 or higher and has at least two entries at each of levels 2 through 5. Each represents all six kinds and includes a template task; compute also includes a generic computer task. The first task has multiple dependent visible definitions or a measured failure.
  • paths.six_kinds_one_world: {world: "integer@1", steps: [...]}. Six authored value checks, in object, operation, combinator, law, bridge, observation order. Each step has name, ASCII definition, executable body (kernel-node JSON), and depends_on names already defined earlier in the same path. The operation uses the object; the combinator uses that operation; the law rewrites that combinator; the bridge preserves that law while mapping into the object; the observation reads the bridge and operation. four_kinds was removed: its tasks were from unrelated worlds with no dependency edges. These authored steps have angle compute and level 3; unlike ladder levels, their level is not measured by the generic difficulty scorer.

docs.title: Task entries
docs.text:
Every task has id, world, kind, angle, level, purpose, label, prompt, answer_format, and grading. grading says the entry is graded offline by the exact grader. purpose is one spoiler-free English sentence. prompt is the generator's original ASCII English prompt. Legacy operations use the shared opulse.tasks_v2.ascii printer, including to_ascii_definition for definition answers. The generic computer prompt uses a readable machine-program rendering; it does not contain raw machine-node JSON. The label is legacy-v1 operations world only for the old operation generators; tasks from the kind generators and the generic computer adapter are atoms-v2.

The public file contains no references, outcomes, solutions, per-answer hashes, or other answer checks. Native tasks and references are deterministically generated at build time into the ignored build/challenge_v2/grading.json (override with OPULSE_CHALLENGE_GRADING). Rebuild it with:

PYTHONPATH=src python -m opulse.tasks_v2.challenge_grade --build

The grader also builds it on first use when absent and verifies the bytes against grading_sha256 before grading. Do not publish the build file. Run PYTHONPATH=src python -m opulse.tasks_v2.challenge_grade '<entry id>' '<JSON answer>' from the repository root to print a JSON verdict such as {"correct": true}. The CLI uses the native exact task grader for ladder entries and the private reference for authored path steps. Definition answers retain all native structural and scope obligations. A public browser cannot grade this catalogue without an offline grading service; do not copy the private data or its answers to the browser.

The exporter uses private closure and shape signatures to select distinct entries; these signatures are not published. A future exporter can register another kind or world by adding one callable to SOURCES.

docs.title: Difficulty
docs.text:
opulse.tasks_v2.difficulty.measure returns the frozen feature record: depth, definitions, steps, branching, recursion, failures, solutions, distractor_closeness, and family-specific fields. For legacy operations the score counts the visible dependency graph, the reference's unfolded evaluation steps, Bottom outcomes over explicit scopes, and alternatives differing on at most two description probes. For the other kinds it uses the visible layer labels and opened definitions, the reference body's node count, the size of example and held-out evidence, visible branches/recursion, Bottom in the published reference or examples, solution count, and number of competing options. The computer adapter additionally counts the actual reference execution on its visible input. These measure structural work rather than subjective solving time. Example and held-out evidence costs for the other kinds are static node-count estimates, not runtime machine-step measurements. Laws additionally count rewrite and refused steps, variables, scope assignments, statement tree depth, required savings and distinct values in induction tables. Bridges count interface pairs, partial-domain guards, map tree depth, candidate bridges and scope assignments. Templates count parameter slots, shown instantiations, the expanded body structure and tested examples, candidates or held-out cases.

The integer score is 2*min(depth,4) + min(definitions//3,4) + min(steps//8,4) + 2*branch + 3*recursion + 2*min(failures,2) + min(max(solutions-1,0),3) + min(distractor_closeness,3), plus capped family-specific terms: 2*min(rewrite_steps,4) + 2*min(refused_steps,2) + min(variables,3) + min(scope_size//4,3) + min(statement_depth//2,3) + min(saving//2,3) + min(max(distinct_expressions-1,0),3) + 2*min(interface_pairs,3) + 2*partial_domain + min(map_depth,3) + min(candidate_bridges,3) + 2*min(parameters,3) + 2*min(instantiations,3) + min(expanded_depth//2,3) + min(obligations,4). The fixed cutoffs 3, 6, 9, 12 give levels 1 through 5; this export's complete seeded pool has distribution 144, 275, 249, 207, 287 respectively. The at-least-two-per-level selection rejects constant single-node rules, trivial operation closures, repeated shapes/closures, and prompts that cannot be rendered as ASCII.

docs.title: Run a definition, then inspect a boundary
docs.text:
Clone the repository, install the project's Python dependencies with python -m pip install -e ., and run the code below from its root. This example uses a local core operation; it does not load a published world. It parses and prints a declaration, evaluates it under two fuel limits, then runs a fixpoint combinator. See the installation instructions for setup.

Executable (core SHA-256 d5923c44986a)

Backed by tests/test_atoms2_research.py::test_quickstart_printed_output_matches_real_fixture in this checkout. Run from the repository root with the checkout's Python environment and installed project dependencies. inc is a local, bounded layer-0 operation; this example is not a verified world export.

docs.title: 1. Parse, evaluate, and cut the trace
docs.text:
The code below is one command. It creates no files. The local advance operation calls the capped inc operation twice, so the fixpoint reaches 5 from 0. The machine notation printer forms the fixpoint expression shown in the output; its head and arguments are separated there for readability. The Python API prints the unchanged ASCII machine storage form; the site displays v3 formulas through a world legend. This local example has no published world legend, so its code and captured output remain machine notation.

PYTHONPATH=src python - <<'PY'
from opulse.atoms import nodes, notation
from opulse.atoms.boundary import Boundary, flatten_calls
from opulse.atoms.combinators import combinator_defn, counter_atoms, fix_atoms, fix_spec
from opulse.atoms.kernel import Atom, Defn, DictScope, FnRef, Limits, call

declaration = notation.parse_definition('op advance(x: Int) -> Int = inc(inc(x)) L1')
print('declaration:', notation.print_definition(declaration))
scope = DictScope(
    atoms=[Atom('inc', 1, lambda value: min(value + 1, 5)), *counter_atoms(), *fix_atoms()],
    defns=[Defn(declaration.name, ('x',), declaration.body), combinator_defn(fix_spec())],
)
for fuel in (1, 2):
    run = call('advance', (1,), scope, limits=Limits(fuel=fuel))
    print('advance fuel', fuel, ':', run.outcome, 'layer-0 steps:', run.steps)

expression = nodes.Call('fix', (nodes.Lit(FnRef('advance')), nodes.Lit(0), nodes.Lit(6)))
context = {'kinds': {'fix': 'combinator'}, 'op_arity': {'fix': 1}}
text = notation.print_expr(expression, context)
assert notation.parse_expr(text, context) == expression
print('fixpoint head:', text.split('(')[0])
print('fixpoint arguments:', '(' + text.split('(', 1)[1])
run = call('fix', (FnRef('advance'), 0, 6), scope, trace=True)
print('result:', run.outcome, 'layer-0 steps:', run.steps)
for label, boundary in (('closed', Boundary.unfold_none()),
                        ('open', Boundary.unfold_all())):
    visible = flatten_calls(run.trace, boundary)
    charged = sum(frame.steps for frame in visible)
    assert run.trace.outcome == run.outcome and charged == run.steps
    print(label, 'boundary:', len(visible), 'visible calls;',
          'outcome:', run.trace.outcome, 'charged steps:', charged)
PY

Observed output in this checkout:

declaration: op advance(x: Int) -> Int = inc(inc(x)) L1
advance fuel 1 : Unknown(resource='fuel') layer-0 steps: 1
advance fuel 2 : Ok(value=3) layer-0 steps: 2
fixpoint head: @fix[advance]
fixpoint arguments: (0, 6)
result: Ok(value=5) layer-0 steps: 19
closed boundary: 1 visible calls; outcome: Ok(value=5) charged steps: 19
open boundary: 19 visible calls; outcome: Ok(value=5) charged steps: 19

Unknown(fuel) means the first call stopped after one charged step, not that it produced a correct answer. The fixpoint checks for a stable state and stops at 5. Closing the trace hides 18 calls but preserves its outcome and 19 charged layer-0 steps. This is one executable input, not an exhaustive check of the combinator.

docs.title: Give a finite world a contract
docs.text:
A world begins with typed layer-0 objects, operations, combinators, and observations. Its declaration also fixes which kinds may be invented, canonicalization rules, per-agent visibility, full-state judging, fuel, generator moves, and the evidence required for promotion. In ASCII machine notation, the Python core parses law (#law) and bridge (~bridge) definitions and checks scoped rewrites and interface commutation. The proposed SQL-style contract on this page does not run browser law or bridge checks. See the semantics for the v2 grammar.

Designed example

The proposed SQL-style contract below has no database-backed evaluator or public builder CLI. Start with the executable core-only quickstart instead. The circuits@1 declaration is a separate source example.

docs.title: A transaction, seen from two sides
docs.text:
LEARNER / ALLOWED

Designed example

State: a finite, typed table with at most four rows and a transaction log. Actions: insert a row, update a key, commit or roll back a transaction. Observations: a rows probe reveals only rows permitted to the acting user; a last-error probe reveals a documented error class. The learner may define a retry combinator for updates only if the world's open kinds and allowed nodes permit it.

These names are a proposed interface, not installed primitives.

JUDGE / REQUIRED

Designed example

Judge against the entire table, commit history, ownership policy and transaction state, including hidden rows. Canonicalize row order without changing query results. Record Bottom(duplicate_key) on an invalid insert and Unknown(fuel) when the fixed budget is exhausted. Charge the exact layer-0 calls after any promoted definition is unfolded.

A filtered row view cannot substitute for full-state equivalence.

docs.title: Contract checklist
docs.text:
Declare Specify and test Values and bounds Types for keys, rows, log entries, users; finite key/value sets; maximum rows, turns, and fuel. No unbounded streams. Given atoms Object constructors and valid/canon functions; operation inputs, outputs, costs and failure reasons; allowed kernel nodes. Inventions Declare open_kinds explicitly; check dependencies and reject closed kinds. Python implements law, bridge and template checks, but this designed SQL world has no runnable declaration or evidence. Visibility Allowed probes and channels for each user, including errors, renders, traces, steps, feedback, and memory. A full-state judge view stays separate. Evidence Exact check method and domain, independent reference comparison, definition/world hashes, layer-0 cost and scope-carrying promotion contract. Seed sampled tests but never promote from samples alone. Reproduction Versioned schema and state codec, fixed generator seeds and moves, split IDs, oracle revision and golden traces.

Reference-system cross-check, planned: for each finite transaction sequence, run the identical operation sequence against an isolated SQL engine in a pinned version. Compare committed rows, rollback behavior, order-insensitive query results, and error classes with the Opulse adapter. Explicitly reconcile SQL null, transaction isolation, and order semantics before claiming equivalence. A difference is a failing test, not a reward to average away. A RISC-V adapter is another candidate research track, not a shipped world.

docs.title: Read a mark
docs.text:
In a display formula, a mark is one glyph with an optional index. The glyph tells you the kind: a suit or shape is an operation, a double-struck capital an object, a Greek capital a combinator, a hatted capital an observation, ≡ a law and ↝ a bridge. In the fixed example legend, ♦₆ is an operation named f6. Digits starting 1 to 9 select a defined atom; digits starting with 0 number an overflow given when a kind runs out of unindexed glyphs; a letter identifies a parameter slot, as in ♦ₐ. No index means a given, such as ℤ. A real world's legend identifies its own marks and signatures; you cannot infer its names from this example's numbers.

Read the bracket after the mark before reading its arguments. Parentheses ( ) pass values, square brackets [ ] pass atoms, and angle brackets ⟨ ⟩ pass hidden state. In C8, Θ₁[♦ₐ] x = { ♦ₐ (♦ₐ x) } defines a combinator that applies its operation slot twice. C9, Θ₁[♡₄₅] 3 ⇒ 12, supplies a defined operation to that slot. In C11, Ô₁⟨s⟩ = { not Ŵ⟨s⟩ and not Û⟨s⟩ }, angle brackets identify the state read by granted probes. A signature line such as (+) : ℤ × ℤ → ℤ gives input and output types; a formula line such as a ♦₆ b = { (a @) * b } gives a definition. A left superscript on a header identifies its layer, not a different kind.

The site's formulas use these marks. The source declarations and historical exports remain in ASCII machine notation; the v3-ASCII copy spelling, such as \dia_6 for ♦₆, maps each display token back to ASCII. Read the notation reference for the complete table and all C examples.

A world need not open every kind for invention. If only operation is open, you can define new operations but still use given objects, combinators and observations. This is the classic Opulse case. Other worlds open several kinds; laws and bridges are listed when a world opens them. Filter by open kinds in the Worlds catalog.

The grammar kernel encodes its word value as a token sequence with the same tokens. The infix grouping and proposed tree and postfix forms are schematic, not core output.

docs.title: Six kinds
docs.text:
A world declares its layer 0 as given; later definitions depend on earlier layers. Each world decides which kinds are open to invention. A mark is one glyph plus an index: suits and shapes for operations, double-struck capitals for objects, Greek capitals for combinators, hatted capitals for observations, ≡ for laws and ↝ or ⇝ for bridges. A template retains its kind's mark and takes atom parameters in brackets; new kinds can use ◈ with a kind-number superscript. These shapes identify kinds without relying on color.

Digits starting 1 to 9 mean a defined atom; digits starting with 0 number an overflow given when a kind runs out of unindexed glyphs; a letter means a parameter slot; no index means a given; a splice index ⌞e⌟ names the atom computed by e. A left superscript on a signature mark gives its layer; a prime on an observation reads its previous value. Each world has a legend mapping marks to names, kinds and signatures. The fixed symbol-to-ASCII map does not depend on that legend.

A mark can sit between two values, before one value or after it. Parentheses group compound operands; a mark binds more tightly than an arithmetic or comparison sign. A mark followed by ( ) takes values, [ ] takes atoms, and ⟨ ⟩ takes hidden state. Brackets immediately after a mark belong to that mark, regardless of spaces. = defines, == compares, ⇒ gives a result, : introduces a signature, and ⊢ attaches a checked condition. A law mark between expressions is one rewrite step. Objects use ∈ and ∣ to refine a set, × for product, and ↾ to seal an interface; ⌜ ⌝ quotes a definition.

Designed example

The six declarations are illustrations, not checked examples. The ASCII machine notation is preserved here for parser users.

  • Object: obj Frac = Quot[Pair<Int, Int>, reduce] L2 gives Frac<1, 2>, a typed value.
  • Operation: op cost(r: Route) -> Int = sum_weights(r) L2 gives cost(route), a computed value. In the roads world, cost adds the road weights along a route (12 for A, D, F, H, K, L); its recorded body reads the route's graph and vertices through member operations that the ASCII printer cannot print yet, so this line is a schematic.
  • Combinator: comb @twice[step: A -> A](state: A) -> A = step(step(state)) L4 gives @twice[step](state), two applications in this illustration.
  • Observation: obs ?top{body} = ?visible{body} L2 gives ?top{body}, a read of a permitted probe if that probe is granted.
  • Law: law #mul_comm: eq(mul(a, b), mul(b, a)) for a: Int, b: Int L3 illustrates a rewrite declaration; by #mul_comm needs a separate scope check.
  • Bridge: bridge ~to_frac: MyFrac -> Frac = make(x) L4 gives ~to_frac(x), a proposed translation.

opulse.atoms.laws checks a law on a declared domain and replays a promoted rewrite against its scope and layer-0 outcome. opulse.atoms.bridges checks translation and interface commutation on a declared domain; inputs outside a partial bridge's domain return Bottom(outside_domain). See the glossary for exact spelling.

docs.title: Typed expressions
docs.text:
Values are finite Int, Text or Card(sort, tag, fields) trees in the Python API. Objects can compose forms, refine a base with valid and canon, or seal their representation. The display uses infix defined marks as well as given arithmetic and comparison signs. The machine parser keeps its named calls such as lt(a, b) and eq(a, b); they are storage syntax, not the visible notation.

The implemented kernel has Var, Lit, Call, Let, ordered Case, measured or fuel-limited Rec, and Blocks/Jump. Call takes a name and typed arguments; Let binds an evaluated outcome; Case selects its first true arm. See opulse.atoms.nodes for entry points and docs/spec/atoms-v2.md in the repository for the node fields.

docs.title: Evaluation and accounting
docs.text:
Evaluation returns Ok(value), Bottom(reason) for a domain failure, or Unknown(resource) for an exhausted budget. Unknown never counts as correct. In atoms-v2, arguments evaluate left to right and stop on the first non-Ok outcome. A failing evaluated condition aborts Case; later arms cost nothing. Observations use only granted probes. A judge uses its declared full-state judge view, not a learner-visible projection or reward.

Charged layer-0 steps count evaluated operations and jumps, plus canonicalization where declared. A promoted definition can appear as one visible step without erasing its layer-0 cost. Memoization (reuse of a cached subresult) saves executed work while this kernel charges the same steps as the plain unfolding. An exact cost needs a run and a versioned input, not a count of collapsed trace labels.

docs.title: Four invariants
docs.text:
1. A definition unfolds to layer 0 with the same result, including failure and resource behavior under equal accounting.
  2. A boundary changes what the trace shows, not the outcome or charged layer-0 cost.
  3. Observations never alter facts. The judge compares the declared full-state view.
  4. Promotion carries a definition's content identity, contract, verification method and scope. Seeded samples alone never authorize promotion.

docs.text: Each panel below replays a real kernel run. Open a definition to see its layer-0 calls. The badge identifies the core revision; these runs are not exhaustive verification of the general modes.

docs.title: Templates and meta
docs.text:
Definitions pass through written, checked, callable, verified and, when eligible, promoted. Record kind, origin, layer, dependencies, body, evidence, contract and cost.

Designed example

In the fixed C6 example, 𝕂₄[𝕏ₜ, ♦ₐ] = 𝕏ₜ / ♦ₐ is a quotient template; 𝔻₁ = 𝕂₄[𝕋₅[ℤ, ℤ], ♢₉] is one instance. A checked template family does not automatically verify every instance. Each instance needs separate evidence and can unfold through its template and arguments.

Designed example

A proposed code object holds a finite definition; quote captures code and evaluation requires finite fuel. Changing code makes a new content hash and detaches earlier evidence. Promoted definitions remain immutable. The atoms-v2/0.5 specification does not certify a quote/eval runner; this paragraph describes a design proposal.

docs.title: Clock input: what changed from v1 to v2
docs.text:
Legacy-v1

The committed clock world export has a golden case: add(11, 3) expects 2. KernelEngine loads the published Legacy-v1 registry.

Executable

Run this from the repository root with PYTHONPATH=src. The separate clock@2 declaration in worlds/decl/clock@2.json supplies the hour entry rule. The v2 calls run the declared add through its input edges, so each input is reduced to an hour on entry.

import json
from dataclasses import replace
from pathlib import Path

from opulse.atoms.golden import KernelEngine, iter_cases
from opulse.tasks_v2 import templates

source = Path("docs/assets/data/worlds/clock.json")
world = json.loads(source.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
case = next(case for case in iter_cases("clock", main_only=True)
            if case.kind == "atom_example" and case.operator == "add")
engine = KernelEngine()
state = engine.load(world)
actual = engine.run(state, case).output
assert actual == case.expected_output
print("published add(11, 3):", actual)
print("legacy add(14, 0):", engine.run(state, replace(case, inputs=(14, 0))).output)

clock = templates.library("clock@2")
add = next(operation for operation in clock.world.operations if operation.name == "add")
assert all(edge.sort == "hour" and edge.enter == "normalize" for edge in add.inputs)
for inputs in ((14, 0), (11, 3)):
    result = clock.run("add", inputs).outcome
    print(f"v2 add{inputs}:", result.value.fields[0])

Output from this fixture, recomputed in tests/test_site_ascii.py:

published add(11, 3): 2
legacy add(14, 0): 2
v2 add(14, 0): 2
v2 add(11, 3): 2

The first line checks the published case against its committed expected output. The second evaluates an additional input with the legacy registry; it is not a golden case. The v2 lines run the declared operation: 14 enters as hour 2, so add(14, 0) is 2, and add(11, 3) wraps to 2. They are live runs, not a regenerated v2 golden fixture.

The declared v2 hour in worlds/decl/clock@2.json is a refined integer, and each add input has enter: normalize. Section 14 of docs/spec/atoms-v2.md specifies the same rule. The run uses the clock world's declaration, not the designed template declaration obj Hour = Quot[Int, mod12] given.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text:
These terms apply to atoms-v2. Display formulas have a separate v3-ASCII copy spelling. Copying does not verify a designed declaration. The Python core parses and checks laws and bridges, but this table does not run those checks. The semantics give evaluation rules, the notation reference gives exact symbols, and the versioned specification describes the implemented subset.

Designed example

The illustrative declarations in this table are not verified runs.

Term Meaning and spelling Atom A given or invented object, operation, combinator, observation, law or bridge. The old operation-only meaning belongs to legacy-v1. Object A typed value or form, for example 𝔻₁(2, 4). It may compose, refine or seal its representation. Operation A typed computation such as a ♦₆ b. Given comparisons use binary signs. Combinator A way to assemble computations, such as Θ₁[♡₄₅] 3. Observation A read of granted probes or remembered observations, such as Ô₁⟨s⟩. It is not hidden truth. Law A statement checked on its declared input scope, such as ≡₁; checking 8-bit inputs would not certify all integers. Bridge A translation checked against its declared interface and domain, such as ↝₁(m). Mark One glyph from a kind family, optionally carrying an index, layer or prime. The example mark ♦₆ is an operation. Index Digits starting 1 to 9 select a defined atom; digits starting with 0 number an overflow given when a kind runs out of unindexed glyphs; a letter identifies a slot; no index means given; a splice computes the reference. Slot An atom parameter, not a value: ♦ₐ stands for an operation passed to a template or combinator. Given / invented A given is a layer-0 atom; its mark normally has no index, as with ℤ. Invented definitions have layers 1, 2 and so on. A closed kind cannot be invented in that world. Splice A computed atom placed in the mark's index: ♦⌞e⌟. Layer superscript A left superscript on a header mark records its dependency layer: ¹♠₃ is at layer 1. Legend A per-world map from marks to names, kinds, layers and signatures. Its assignments do not alter the global display-to-ASCII token mapping. Display form The site-facing Unicode spelling of a formula, for example ♦₆. ASCII storage form The unchanged machine declarations in exports and datasets. V3-ASCII (\dia_6) is a separate, one-to-one copy spelling of the display form, not the machine declaration syntax. Layer A dependency level. A higher layer can depend on earlier definitions of any open kind, not only operations. Template A typed family such as 𝕂₄[𝕏ₜ, ♦ₐ]; its instances need their own evidence. Probe / judge view A probe is a permitted read interface. The judge view decides correctness from full state, which may be hidden from a learner. Result / outcome Ok(value) succeeds, Bottom(reason) is a domain failure, and Unknown(resource) is exhaustion and never correct. Undefined NaN belongs to Legacy-v1 only. Reward A task-specific score or projection. Equal rewards do not prove equal full states or outcomes. Evidence / scope A record of method (exhaustive, bounded, seeded sampled), domain, world version and contract. Scope states exactly what was checked. Verification / promotion Verification checks the contract on the stated scope. Promotion lets an eligible verified definition be reused as one visible step with that scope; sampling alone cannot authorize it. Boundary / unfold A boundary selects which definitions to show as one step. Unfolding expands to layer-0 work without changing outcome or charged cost. Fuel A limit on charged layer-0 work. Exhaustion gives Unknown(fuel), not a domain failure.

docs.title: Observation is not truth
docs.text:
Executable

The shadows world export, version 1, grants the top and side probes. Two distinct volumes built with its host constructors have the same top projection. Run this from the repository root with PYTHONPATH=src:

from opulse.worlds_v2.shadows.deep_hosts import front, to_card, top

first = to_card(((1, 2, 0), (4, 5, 1)))
second = to_card(((1, 2, 3), (4, 5, 1)))
print("same full state:", first == second)
print("same top view:", top(first) == top(second))
print("same front view:", front(first) == front(second))

Output, computed at build time from the host functions:

same full state: False
same top view: True
same front view: False

The export grants learners top and side, not front; the front comparison is an external check, not a learner action. A learner reading only ?top{body} cannot distinguish this pair. The judge view is full state, so a matching observation does not establish equality. This is a host-level computation on constructed values, not a kernel verification record. The export has no sealed object pair: Volume is given and unsealed. Observation rules explain the boundary between probes and truth.

Designed example

To teach this ambiguity with sealed values, a future world could define a sealed volume object. It could expose only a top-view observation for distinct hidden bodies that share a top view. This extension is not in the linked shadows historical export. Design record: shadows world, depth pass (11-04). That record proposes projection-only learner views; the seal is an additional proposal.

Read the grammar | Inspect claim sources

docs.title: Notation v3
docs.text: Notation v3 is the site's formula notation. It has two spellings of the same token stream: a Unicode display form and a token-for-token v3-ASCII copy form. The Python machine declaration language is separate and unchanged. Definitions in exports, datasets and training data retain that machine notation; the site generates display formulas from it and copies v3-ASCII rather than substituting an ASCII machine declaration for a visible formula.

docs.title: Reading a formula
docs.text:
1. One atom has one mark: a glyph family indicates its kind and the index identifies its reference. Operations use suits and shapes, objects double-struck capitals, combinators Greek capitals, observations hatted capitals, laws ≡, and bridges ↝ or ⇝. Templates use the family of the kind they produce. An additional kind can use ◈ with a superscript kind number.
  2. Digits starting 1 to 9 identify a defined atom; digits starting with 0 number an overflow given when a kind runs out of unindexed glyphs. Overflow givens use 01, 02, ... in given order per kind (♦₀₇ copies as \dia_07); 0 alone and 00 prefixes are invalid. A subscript letter is a parameter slot, no index means a given, and a ⌞e⌟ index splices in the atom computed by e. A superscript at the left of a definition header mark denotes its layer; a prime on an observation reads its previous value.
  3. Marks may be infix, prefix or postfix. One free mark fits in a term; group a compound operand with parentheses. Marks bind more tightly than arithmetic and comparison signs. Ordinary binary signs have fixed precedence and are not invented marks.
  4. After a mark, ( ) holds values, [ ] holds atom arguments and produces a derived mark, and ⟨ ⟩ holds hidden state. Adjacent brackets attach to the mark even if spaces intervene. A list [ ] elsewhere is a value, not atom parameters.
  5. = defines; == compares; ⇒ shows a result or, with ?, asks for one; : introduces a signature or a quantified law; ⊢ attaches a checked condition. A law mark between two grouped expressions denotes one rewrite step. A case body uses braces with if and else.
  6. Given signs build objects: ∈ and ∣ refine a set, × makes a product, / quotients by an operation, and ↾ seals an interface. Bracketed atom parameters make a template of any kind; ⌜ ⌝ quotes a statement as a value.

Definitions have formula-only bodies. A signature is a separate line carrying types and, if needed, a layer superscript. The per-world legend supplies the long name, kind and signature associated with each mark. A glyph alone cannot tell you which named atom a world assigned to that mark.

docs.title: World legend assignment
docs.text:
Mark assignment is deterministic for each world. First, given arithmetic, comparison and logic operations with the matching names and arities use their binary signs. Remaining layer-0 givens take unindexed marks of their own kind, in symbol-table order: operations take @ # $ & and then the operation families, objects the double-struck capitals (ℤ and 𝔹 are fixed for integers and booleans), combinators the Greek capitals, observations the hatted capitals. A mark never borrows another kind's family: an operation that reads a field or constructs an object still has an operation mark, and the name of an atom never chooses its glyph. If a kind exhausts its unindexed families, later givens receive leading-zero digit indices 01, 02, ... in given order per kind, without a layer marker.

Defined atoms have a digit index within their kind, ordered by layer and then by their order in the export. They start at 1 per kind and never start with 0: no family-and-index-string pair is reused within a world. Operations choose families by arity: unary marks cycle through down/up filled and open triangles; binary marks cycle through suits; arities zero and three or more cycle through squares, circles, lozenges and stars. Objects cycle through the allowed double-struck capitals, combinators through the Greek table and observations through the hatted table; laws use ≡ and bridges use ↝. Atoms of one kind are told apart by their index. Generated machine names are still names in the legend, not alternative marks.

Each export's legend lists givens in declaration order, then defined atoms in layer and definition order. Each entry includes the ASCII mark, display mark, name, kind, layer, origin and optional signature in both spellings. Within a world, the mapping between name and mark works in both directions. Regeneration depends on the ordered atoms, their kinds, layers and arities, not a hash of unrelated export content. The token mapping between v3-ASCII and display remains global and does not require the world legend.

docs.title: Grammar and printing
docs.text:
Lexing is longest-match and independent of kind. A mark is an optional layer, a family, an optional digit/letter/splice index and optional prime. Binary signs (+ - * / % == != < <= > >= × ∈ ↾ and or not) are separate from marks; @ # $ & are given operation marks. A binary sign stands for an operation value only when immediately before ), , or ], as in Φ₂[+]. Arithmetic and comparison givens use binary signs when their world names and arities match the corresponding built-ins.

From weakest to strongest, expressions use lambda or let, or, and, unary not or ↓, non-chained comparisons and membership, sealing, addition/subtraction, multiplication/division/modulo, product ×, unary minus, then marked terms. A term accepts one free mark; further marked operations need explicit grouping. Mark argument brackets can chain for currying. Statements are expressions optionally followed by a definition, result, signature or law and an optional ⊢ check. Quantified laws may group variables from different domains with commas. Case braces accept a plain value, refinement, or ordered if/else arms. The printer preserves explicit grouping and emits canonical single spacing.

Here e means an expression, mg a mark with zero or more atom-argument brackets, u an operand and items a comma-separated, possibly empty list. The precedence levels above expand to the following statement and term forms:

stmt  := e ('=' e check? | '⇒' e | ':' (signature | '∀' binders '.' e) check?)?
check := '⊢' e | '⊢' '↓' e | '⊢' ('fuel' | 'legacy')
binders := VAR (',' VAR)* '∈' e (',' VAR (',' VAR)* '∈' e)*
e     := 'let' VAR '=' e 'in' e | 'rec' local '=' e check 'in' e
       | 'memo' 'rec' local '=' e check 'in' e | precedence-expression ('↦' e)?
local := mg '(' items ')'
term  := mg (('(' items ')' | '⟨' items '⟩') operand-tail | u | empty)
       | u (mg u?)?
mg    := MARK ('[' items ']')*
u     := VAR | NUM | STR | CONST | '?' | '⊤' | '⊥' | '…'
       | '(' items ')' | '[' items ']' | '⌜' stmt '⌝'
       | '{' e ('}' | '∣' e '}' | (',' ('if' e | 'else') (';' e)?)+ '}')
       | mg ('(' items ')' | '⟨' items '⟩') | program
items := (item (',' item)*)?
item  := e | VAR ':' e | standalone-binary-sign

The local recursion binder must use an operation slot. A leading mark followed by ( ) or ⟨ ⟩ is a call; followed by an operand it is prefix, otherwise it is a bare reference. After an operand, a mark is infix if another operand follows and postfix otherwise. An operand with a second free mark needs parentheses. A bare binary sign is an item only before ), , or ]; - and not require this lookahead to distinguish them from unary operators. These rules apply identically to both spellings.

Published definitions also use these extensions to the base grammar:

Form Rule Strings and literals Double-quoted JSON-escaped ASCII strings; unary negative numbers, including within lists; booleans ⊤ / ⊥. Failure and unknown fail("reason") and unknown("fuel") each take one parenthesized item. Let let x = e in e binds as weakly as lambda; the word in is distinct from membership ∈. Recursion rec ♦ᵣ(x, y) = e ⊢ ↓ m in ♦ᵣ(a, b); measures may instead be fuel or legacy. memo rec memoizes it. A matching tail call may print as self-recursion of the defined mark. Constructor atoms A sort with several forms assigns each form a separate operation mark, such as ♣₄(x, y) or ♣₅(). A sort with exactly one declared form, or one form observed in the export when none is declared, calls its object mark instead: 𝔻₁(2, 4). The legend lists forms and constructor atoms; records accept named fields such as pos: (2, 3). Objects Variants sum forms with +; product uses ×; quotient, refinement, constants and template instances use the forms above. Programs prog (x = 0, y = 1) entry L0 { L0: x := e; jump L1; L1: halt x }; if c jump L1 else L2 terminates conditionally. Labels are uppercase constants with optional digits; other machine labels receive stable L0, L1, ... names. Names Variables start lowercase and may then use letters, digits or _; reserved keywords (let in rec fail unknown memo prog entry jump halt fuel legacy if else and or not) are not variables. The converter appends _ to conflicting or non-lowercase machine names. Constants are capitalised words (E, P1, Metro); a value form without fields whose name is capitalised prints as that constant, so a route reads A, D, F rather than as constructor calls.

Parsing a formula does not check that a mark is used at the right kind. Kind checking must reject semantically invalid forms, even if they parse. The display and ASCII printers produce canonical text; for canonical formulas, parsing either spelling and printing it back preserves the exact text.

docs.title: Provenance
docs.text: Behavioral claims need a versioned artifact, a declared check scope and a reproducible method. Design material is not a check. A projected reward does not prove full-state equivalence. See semantics and research protocols.

docs.title: Claim ledger
docs.text:
Executable

src/opulse/atoms/kernel.py and src/opulse/atoms/values.py implement Ok, Bottom, Unknown and finite limits under atoms-v2/0.5 (docs/spec/atoms-v2.md in the repository). Core input SHA-256: d5923c44986a (first 12 hex digits of the digest of sorted core Python file paths and bytes). This is an implementation claim, not an exhaustive check. A code or contract change needs a new test and claim.

Designed example

shadows.json carries schema opulse.world_v2_export/1, a world version and declaration lock. It does not independently check the glossary's two-body example. A world edit needs a new lock and evidence.

Designed example

Auditable design file, not a checked claim: the published action.json export has SHA-256 file digest {{ A2_ACTION_EXPORT_SHA256 }}. The export stores declaration lock value {{ A2_ACTION_LOCK_WORLD_HASH }}. The stored value matches the declaration hash computed by WorldDecl.world_hash() in this checkout, but neither hash certifies a checker result. The file digest covers the bytes served by the built site, not the unbuilt source file. The downloadable audit template copies the stored lock value and records a proposed method, but its checker revision, seeds, results and changed-claim comparison are null. The executable examples above have versioned run artifacts. This ledger does not yet include an independently checked world-example claim binding a completed checker result to a published file hash. A changed export needs a new digest and a new check.

Executable

The combination-mode panels replay kernel runs exported by tools/atoms2_ui_export.py into docs/assets/js/atoms2/data.js. Each panel shows its recorded input, outcome, exact layer-0 steps and core SHA-256; the memo panel also distinguishes charged steps from executed work. These are executable input traces, not exhaustive or bounded verification of the general modes. The export does not provide a checker scope or verified world hash for those broader claims. The panel's core SHA-256 identifies the exported run, which may differ from this page's build-time core SHA-256.

Legacy-v1

Historical benchmarks are in repository history, not atoms-v2 throughput evidence. A v2 benchmark needs hardware, seed, code version, inputs and repeat.

A verification record should contain a definition content hash, world hash and version, method, scope, seed if sampled, layer-0 cost, judge view, outcome and checker artifact. Bounded evidence covers only its stated bound. A seeded sample can be stored but cannot license promotion. Editing a definition or its dependencies gives a new identity and detaches old evidence; promotion never survives an edit silently.

docs.title: Lineage and versions
docs.text: The earlier published site taught operator-only worlds. This published interface is now legacy-v1. The atoms-v2 design covers six definable kinds, templates and meta definitions. The versioned core specification describes an implemented subset; do not treat older operator-only results as evidence for the extensions. Historical v1 release notes remain in repository history under docs/about/changelog.md.
